summary: Specifies IS-IS autoconfiguration mechanisms, including self-generation of the System ID, detection of duplicate IDs and resolution of duplicates. It provides limited IS-IS functions for networks where plug-and-play setup is expected.

plainLanguage.summary: New routers pick their own name tags when they join. If two choose the same one, they notice and one picks again.

questions: how does is-is detect duplicate system id
subtitle: How IS-IS routers can pick their own identity and sort out clashes with no manual setup.

tldr.problem: IS-IS normally needs an administrator to give each router a unique identity and configure it, which is a burden in small plug-and-play networks.
tldr.mechanism: An autoconfigured router uses fixed defaults, builds its own System ID, and advertises a Router-Fingerprint TLV so that two routers with the same System ID can detect the clash and one of them picks a new ID.
tldr.outcome: IS-IS can run with no user configuration in small networks (10s of devices), with limits: level-1 only, one instance, no multi-area routing.

today: RFC 8196 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2017. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8196 defines mechanisms that let IS-IS configure itself. The aim is to reduce the management burden, especially where plug-and-play device configuration is required. The pieces are default configuration, System ID self-generation, System ID duplication detection and resolution, and guidance on a few existing TLVs.

The scope is deliberately narrow. It supports both IPv4 and IPv6, but it does not support multiple IS-IS instances, multi-area and level-2 routing, or interworking with other routing protocols. It is intended for small (10s of devices) and unmanaged deployments and is not recommended for larger ones.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way for a few small routers to set themselves up, like kids in a clubhouse picking their own seats. It is meant for small groups, not huge ones.

sections.title: Default Configuration and NET Generation
sections.content:
An autoconfigured router MUST pick each interface type from its Layer 2 capability (Ethernet becomes broadcast, PPP becomes point-to-point) and MUST run as level-1 only. originatingLSPBufferSize is set to 512 and MaxAreaAddresses is set to 3. It MUST use extended IS reachability (TLV 22) and IP reachability (TLV 135), and MUST NOT use TLV 2, TLV 128 or TLV 130, which MUST be ignored on receipt.

A router is identified by a Network Entity Title (NET). In autoconfiguration the area address is 13 octets of all 0s, and the System ID is 6 octets. The System ID must be unique in the area and SHOULD stay stable after it is first generated: interface changes, reboots, firmware updates or configuration changes SHOULD NOT alter it. A change as part of collision resolution MUST be supported, and implementations SHOULD let a user-initiated system reset clear it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every self-configuring router starts with the same simple settings and invents its own 6-part name tag. It keeps that tag unless there is a clash.

sections.title: The Router-Fingerprint TLV
sections.content:
The Router-Fingerprint TLV is type 15. It is similar to the Router-Hardware-Fingerprint TLV in RFC 7503 but adds a one-octet Flags field. The S flag means the router is in startup mode. The A flag means it is operating in autoconfiguration mode. The other flag bits are reserved: they MUST be zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver. The fingerprint itself is 32 or more octets.

A router in autoconfiguration mode MUST include the TLV with the A flag set in its IS-IS Hellos and in LSP #0, and MUST ignore hellos that lack it. If an LSP #0 arrives without the TLV, or with the A flag clear, the LSP is flooded normally but the sender's whole LSP set is ignored in the Decision Process. The TLV MUST NOT appear in an LSP with a non-zero number, and is ignored if received there.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is a secret-ish stamp each router attaches to its messages. Two flags say "I am brand new" and "I am a self-configuring router".

sections.title: Startup Mode and Adjacencies
sections.content:
When a router starts in autoconfiguration mode, both the S and A flags MUST be set. Only LSP #0 is generated, and IS or IP/IPv6 reachability TLVs MUST NOT be included in it. The router stays in startup mode for a minimum time (recommended to be 1 minute), and leaves it once that time has passed and full LSP database synchronization is achieved with all neighbors in the UP state. It then clears the S flag and MAY advertise reachability and generate LSPs with a non-zero number.

The purpose is to keep System ID changes away from a fully operational router: a router in startup mode is not yet used for forwarding, so a change costs little.

Autoconfigured routers MUST NOT form adjacencies with routers that are not in autoconfiguration mode. The all-zero area address makes a mix-up unlikely, and the A flag check adds protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A new router first listens quietly for a minute before it starts telling others how to reach things. If it has to change its name tag, nobody is bothered yet.

sections.title: Detecting and Resolving Duplicate System IDs
sections.content:
A duplicate with a neighbor is detected when a hello carries the local System ID but a Router-Fingerprint that differs from the local one. A duplicate with a non-neighbor is detected the same way from an LSP #0. One of the two systems MUST then generate a new System ID and restart the protocol.

  • If only one router is in startup mode (S flag set), that router changes.
  • If both or neither are in startup mode, the router with the numerically smaller fingerprint changes. The comparison goes octet by octet, and if one fingerprint is a prefix of the other, the shorter one is smaller.
  • If the fingerprints are identical and the clash was seen in hellos, both routers change.
  • If they are identical and the clash was seen in LSP #0, the DD-LSP procedure applies.
sections.plainLanguage: If two kids have the same name tag, the one who just arrived changes theirs. If both arrived at the same time, the one with the smaller secret number changes.

sections.title: When Both System ID and Fingerprint Match
sections.content:
Resources for making identifiers may be scarce at startup, so both values can collide. The RFC calls an LSP with the same System ID and fingerprint that is not identical to the local copy (newer sequence number, or same number with a valid but different checksum) a DD-LSP. In the benign case a restarted router sees its own old LSPs. In the pathological case two different routers keep overwriting each other's LSP with higher sequence numbers, and synchronization never completes.

The procedure uses DD-state, DD-count, a DD-timer (recommended 60 seconds) and DD-max (recommended 3). The first DD-LSP sets DD-state to TRUE, starts the timer and sets the count to 1. Each later DD-LSP increments the count. When the count reaches DD-max, the router MUST generate a new System ID and Router-Fingerprint and restart. When the timer expires, DD-state returns to FALSE. Adding the next LSP sequence number to the fingerprint is suggested to add entropy.
sections.plainLanguage: If two routers keep shouting the same thing over each other, a router counts how often it happens in a minute. After three times it decides it must be the one clashing and picks a new name.

sections.title: Generating IDs and Using Other TLVs
sections.content:
Seeds for identifiers include MAC addresses, configured IP addresses, hardware IDs, serial numbers, the system clock and received packets. The RFC recommends an IEEE 802 48-bit MAC address as the initial System ID. It specifies no method to regenerate the System ID or to generate the fingerprint. For small devices such as home routers it suggests the MAC address as System ID and a pseudorandom number from another seed as the fingerprint.

On TLVs: routers SHOULD offer an option to configure a single password for HMAC-MD5 authentication (RFC 5304), SHOULD default to a high metric (for example 100000) so that manually configured adjacencies are preferred, and MAY advertise the Dynamic Name TLV (TLV 137) with the System ID appended to keep names unique.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers build their name tags from things that are already unique, like the serial number printed on the device.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Without cryptographic authentication, an attacker can inject a PDU that falsely signals a duplicate System ID and trigger a protocol restart. The RFC also notes that authentication is incompatible with autoconfiguration, since it needs some manual configuration.

It points to physical security on wired deployments, where unwanted routers usually cannot connect, and to link-layer authentication on wireless ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could shout "you have my name!" and make routers change their tags. Locking the door or the Wi-Fi keeps pranksters out.
